title: The Great Wall of China: One Wall, or Many?
description: Two hosts unpack how the Great Wall was built, how long it really is, and which famous claims about it are myths.
critical_facts: twenty-one thousand, one hundred and ninety-six kilometers
sources: UNESCO World Heritage List, The Great Wall (inscribed 1987), https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/438
State Administration of Cultural Heritage of China, 2012 survey: 21,196 km of walls
Yang, F. et al. (2010), Accounts of Chemical Research 43(6): sticky rice-lime mortar
NASA Earth Observatory, 'Great Wall of China' (2005) on visibility from orbit
Xinhua (2003): Yang Liwei did not see the Great Wall from orbit

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Here's a confession on behalf of the whole world. The Great Wall of China is not really one wall.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Hold on. It's the most famous wall on Earth, and it isn't one wall?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: It's a network. Different states and dynasties built walls over roughly two thousand years. Some ran side by side, and some were rebuilt on top of older ones.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: This is Long Story Short, one big subject in fifteen minutes. I'm Maya. Daniel has spent far too many summers walking on that wall, and today he gets to ruin my school facts.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Only the wrong ones. Let's start with who began it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: My guess is one emperor with a very big plan.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Close, but late. The earliest walls go back to rival states in the seventh century BC. The big moment comes in two hundred and twenty-one BC. That's when the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, unified China. He had the northern walls joined up and extended against the nomads of the steppe.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So I picture stone walls with towers, like on the postcards.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Not yet. Most early walls were rammed earth. Workers packed soil and gravel into wooden frames, layer by layer, until it was as hard as rock. In the western deserts, the Han dynasty even used layers of sand and willow branches.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Sand and sticks. Then the postcard wall is much younger than I thought.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Much younger. It's mostly the Ming dynasty, which ruled from thirteen sixty-eight to sixteen forty-four. The Ming rebuilt the wall in brick and stone, with thousands of watchtowers. The famous sections near Beijing, like Badaling and Mutianyu, are Ming work.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Now the number everybody asks about. How long is it?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: In twenty twelve, China's heritage agency finished a national survey. Counting every branch and every dynasty, it found twenty-one thousand, one hundred and ninety-six kilometers.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: That's more than half the way around the Earth. I don't believe it.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: You shouldn't, not as one line. That's the total of many walls. The Ming wall alone is a bit under nine thousand kilometers, from Shanhai Pass at the sea to Jiayu Pass in the desert.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Fine. But I'm keeping my favorite fact. You can see it from space.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Sorry, Maya. The wall is long, but only a few meters wide, and it has the color of the land around it. It's not visible from space with the naked eye. China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, looked for it in two thousand three. He said he couldn't see it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: That hurts. You owe me a true fact that's better.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Sticky rice. Ming builders mixed cooked sticky rice into their lime mortar. In twenty ten, chemists found that a starch from the rice makes the mortar stronger and more water resistant.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So parts of the wall are held together by dinner. I'll take that trade.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: The building itself was no joke, though. Soldiers, farmers and convicts did the work, in huge numbers, and many of them died. There's a folk tale about a woman named Meng Jiangnu. Her husband died on the wall, and she wept so hard that a section collapsed.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: All that work and all those deaths. Did it at least keep invaders out?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: Sometimes. Beacon towers passed warnings hundreds of kilometers, with smoke by day and fire by night. But in sixteen forty-four, a Ming general opened Shanhai Pass, and the Manchu armies rode through.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So the strongest wall still depends on whoever holds the key to the gate.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: That's the real lesson of the wall. It controlled trade, collected taxes and marked the edge of the empire. It only worked with people who chose to defend it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And today? Is it still there to visit?

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: It became a World Heritage Site in nineteen eighty-seven. But wind, rain, farming and souvenir hunters have taken a lot. Reports say about a third of the Ming wall is already gone.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Then here's my plan for my first visit. Mutianyu, because it's restored and quieter than Badaling.

lines.speaker: daniel
lines.text: And there's a toboggan ride down. Just leave the bricks where they are. The wall has lost enough of them to people who loved it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Thanks, Daniel. This was Long Story Short.
